content: The study conducted by Kim in 2012 involved 20 adults aged over 62 years in the Republic of Korea. Another study by Sinha in 2010 included 132 women aged 18 to 40 years in India. Both studies observed a non-significant relationship between indoor temperature and systolic blood pressure but found a significant relationship with diastolic blood pressure. Kim's 2012 study, which had a very small sample size, reported that for every 1°C increase in indoor temperature (above 26°C), there was a measurable effect on body temperature after adjusting for age and sex. However, the quality of evidence was rated very low due to the limited population and imprecision. Ahrenzten's 2016 quasi-experimental study in the USA, involving 57 participants, found that reducing the number of days with indoor temperatures above 27°C improved health and quality of life, reduced emotional distress, and increased sleep duration. Similarly, Quinn's 2017 cohort study of 40 households in the USA supported these findings. However, the evidence quality was rated low due to inconsistencies and imprecision. For mental health, Ahrenzten's 2016 study showed that reducing the number of days with high indoor temperatures corresponded with reduced emotional distress. The evidence quality was rated very low due to the small sample size and limited applicability. A systematic review on indoor heat for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines assessed the impact of indoor temperature on sleep. Ahrenzten (2016), Quinn (2017), and van Loenhout (2016) conducted studies involving 57 participants in the USA, 40 households in the USA, and 113 participants in the Netherlands, respectively. Ahrenzten's study found that reducing high-temperature days increased sleep duration. However, the cohort studies by Quinn and van Loenhout found that higher temperatures were associated with increased sleep problems. The evidence quality was rated low due to inconsistencies. Asamoah's 2018 cross-sectional study in Ghana, involving 1136 women, examined the association between ambient heat exposure and pregnancy outcomes such as miscarriage or stillbirth. The evidence quality was rated very low due to imprecision and limited applicability. For respiratory diseases, Quinn's 2017 cohort study of 40 households in the USA found no association between indoor temperature and respiratory viral infections. Uejio's 2016 case-control study of 764 emergency care patients in the USA provided inconsistent findings. The evidence quality was rated very low due to imprecision and inconsistency. Regarding cardiovascular disease, Fink's 2017 cohort study in Slovenia and Uejio's 2016 case-control study in the USA (764 participants) found that higher heat burden and poor indoor air quality were associated with the expression and aggravation of cardiovascular symptoms. The evidence quality was rated very low due to imprecision and inconsistency. Chen's 2011 study in a climatic chamber with 16 healthy volunteers aged 18–22 years examined the effects of temperature changes on thermal sensation and skin physiological properties. Fang's 2004 study with 30 female subjects in a controlled office environment assessed productivity and thermal comfort under varying temperature and humidity conditions. Jin's 2011 study with 23 healthy volunteers simulated summer and winter conditions to evaluate thermal sensation. Liu's 2008 study with 33 healthy volunteers measured heart rate variability and thermal comfort at different temperatures. Schellen's 2010 study in a climate chamber with 16 male volunteers (8 young adults and 8 older adults) assessed skin and core temperature under stable and transient temperature conditions. Tham's 2004 study with 56 female call center operators evaluated thermal comfort and work performance under different temperature and air velocity conditions.
